subject: business
title: The Value Chain: where costs and margins actually hide
dek: In 1985 Michael Porter argued that competitive advantage does not live in a slogan or a department. It lives in the specific activities a company performs, and in how those activities link. He called the sequence of those activities the value chain. Eleven years later, in Harvard Business Review, he showed that the hardest strategies to copy are ones in which many activities fit together, as at Southwest Airlines and IKEA. This lesson explains the framework first, then follows the companies that rebuilt their chains on purpose.
era: 1985 Competitive Advantage framework, then 1990s cases that made activity systems concrete
honesty: The five primary activities, four support activities, the idea of linkages, and the distinction between a firm's value chain and the larger value system come from Michael E. Porter's 1985 book Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance, as summarised by Harvard Business School's Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness. The claim that strategy is a unique configuration of activities, and the Southwest and IKEA activity-system examples, come from Porter's November–December 1996 Harvard Business Review article 'What Is Strategy?'. The IKEA flat-pack, suburban-store, self-service and hang-tag activity choices, and the Zara speed contrast, come from Joan Magretta's Understanding Michael Porter (Harvard Business Review Press, 2011), which restates Porter's activity-system maps for managers. Dell's direct model and the phrase 'virtual integration' come from Magretta's March–April 1998 HBR interview 'The Power of Virtual Integration'. Zara's two-to-four-week design-to-store cycle and Castellano's stock-as-food remark are reported in BCG's 2015 article 'The Rising Need for Innovation Speed'; the Harvard Business School case ZARA: Fast Fashion (Ghemawat and Nueno) gives the related four-to-five-week new-design and two-week modification figures. The Gillis Lundgren flat-pack story is from Guinness World Records; IKEA Museum notes that earlier self-assembly tables already appeared in the 1953 catalogue. The closing question applying the framework to a small resale shop is our own framing. The lesson contains no images.

sections.title: Strategy without a place to look

blocks.text: By the early 1980s, managers already had a language for rivalry. Porter's own earlier book, Competitive Strategy (1980), had given them the five forces: the pressures from rivals, new entrants, substitutes, suppliers and buyers. That framework answers a market question: how hard is it to make a good return in this industry? It does not answer an internal question: which of our own steps create the advantage, and which just add cost?

Companies often answered that second question with vague strengths. They said they were good at 'service', 'quality' or 'innovation'. Those words are too broad to manage. A customer does not pay for a department name. A customer pays for a sequence of concrete steps: the way materials arrive, the way a product is made or assembled, the way it is shipped, sold and supported afterward. Until those steps are named, a strategy debate stays abstract.

Porter's answer in 1985 was to take the firm apart. Competitive Advantage introduced the value chain: a map of the activities a company performs to design, produce, sell, deliver and support what it offers. Advantage, he argued, comes from performing particular activities more cheaply than rivals, or in ways that create more buyer value, or from managing the links between activities better. Harvard Business School's Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness still presents the tool that way: strategy is the set of choices about how activities are configured and linked.

sections.title: Nine boxes, and the links between them

blocks.text: Porter splits activities into two layers. Primary activities sit on the bottom of the classic diagram and touch the product or service directly. Support activities sit above them and improve the primary ones across the firm.

items: Inbound logistics: receiving, storing and handling inputs. For a manufacturer that means parts and raw materials; for a shop it can mean how inventory arrives and is put away.
Operations: the steps that turn inputs into the finished offer, from factory lines to a restaurant kitchen to the way a software team builds a release.
Outbound logistics: getting the finished offer to the buyer, including warehousing, order fulfilment and delivery.
Marketing and sales: the activities that make buyers aware of the offer and complete the sale, from pricing and advertising to a sales force or a website checkout.
Service: what happens after the sale to keep or raise the product's value, such as installation, repairs, returns, training or customer support.

blocks.text: The four support activities are firm infrastructure (planning, finance, quality systems, general management), human resource management, technology development (including process know-how, not only R&D labs), and procurement (purchasing of inputs across the firm). Margin sits at the end of the chain: it is the difference between the price buyers pay and the total cost of performing all the activities.

Two ideas matter as much as the boxes. The first is linkages. How fast operations can run depends on how inbound logistics feeds them. How cheap outbound logistics can be depends on how products are designed and packed in operations. A change in one activity can raise or lower the cost of another. The second idea is the value system. A company's chain sits inside a larger chain of suppliers upstream and distributors or retailers downstream. Advantage can come from redesigning handoffs across that wider system, not only from polishing steps inside one firm.

people.name: Michael E. Porter
people.text: Harvard Business School professor who introduced five forces in Competitive Strategy (1980) and the value chain in Competitive Advantage (1985), then argued in 'What Is Strategy?' (1996) that lasting advantage comes from unique, interlocking activities.

people.name: Joan Magretta
people.text: Former HBR strategy editor who interviewed Michael Dell in 1998 and later wrote Understanding Michael Porter (2011), which restates value chains and activity-system maps for practicing managers.

sections.title: Why copying one step is not enough

blocks.text: In 'What Is Strategy?' (1996), Porter drew a sharp line between operational effectiveness and strategy. Operational effectiveness means performing similar activities better than rivals: faster machines, leaner processes, fewer defects. Those gains matter, and they are easy for others to copy. Strategy, he wrote, means choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value. The test is not whether you are busy improving. The test is whether your activity choices fit one another so that a rival who copies only one or two of them still fails.

Southwest Airlines is his classic low-cost example. Short-haul routes, frequent departures, a standardised fleet of Boeing 737s, fast gate turns, no meals, no assigned seats and no travel-agent commissions were not separate tips. They reinforced one another. Fast turns needed a simple fleet and a simple boarding process. A simple fleet made maintenance and crew training cheaper. Skipping meals and seat assignments made those fast turns possible. A rival that copied Southwest's fares without copying the whole system would not get the same cost structure.

IKEA works the same way on the retail side. Magretta lists activity choices that look odd one by one and powerful together: company-designed products, outsourced manufacturing under central control, huge suburban stores with parking, a warehouse attached to the showroom, room displays and large hang-tags instead of floor salespeople, flat packs that customers take home and assemble, plus in-store cafeterias and childcare that make long visits workable. Flat packs cut shipping cost and damage. Suburban car access makes self-delivery realistic. Room displays and hang-tags make low staffing workable. Each choice raises the value of the others. That is what Porter means by fit.

IKEA did not invent low prices in furniture. It invented a chain in which the customer performs steps that traditional retailers keep inside the firm. Design stays in-house so products can be made for flat packing and self-assembly. Manufacturing is outsourced but steered centrally. The store is both showroom and warehouse. Marketing leans on the catalogue and the room sets rather than a large sales force. Outbound logistics is partly handed to the shopper's car. Service after the sale is limited by design: the product is meant to work when the customer finishes assembling it. The low price is not a discount campaign. It is the result of moving costs out of activities IKEA refuses to perform the traditional way.

Zara, the main brand of Spain's Inditex, rebuilt the fashion chain around speed rather than lowest factory cost. Traditional apparel retailers often separate design, overseas production and seasonal shipments, which can stretch design-to-store time into many months. Zara keeps designers, procurement and production planners close to store feedback, makes the most time-sensitive items nearby, and ships to stores often. BCG reported a two-to-four-week path from new style to market, and quoted former Inditex CEO José María Castellano: in fashion, stock is like food, it goes bad quick. The Harvard case ZARA: Fast Fashion gives related figures of about four to five weeks for entirely new designs and about two weeks for modifications. Zara accepts trade-offs elsewhere: less advertising than fashion rivals, smaller batches, and production capacity that is not always fully used, so it can react when demand shifts. The advantage is not one hero factory. It is the tight links among store signals, design, production and outbound logistics.

Dell Computer in the 1990s rebuilt the personal-computer chain by cutting out the reseller and building machines to order. In Magretta's 1998 HBR interview, Michael Dell described what she labelled virtual integration: Dell would not own every supplier, but it would coordinate suppliers, assembly and customers through shared information and tight schedules. Customers configured PCs directly. Components arrived late, so Dell carried far less finished-goods inventory than rivals that built to forecast and pushed boxes through distributors. Marketing and sales became a direct channel. Operations became assemble-to-order rather than assemble-to-stock. Outbound logistics shipped from the factory to the buyer. The value-chain point is simple. Dell changed several boxes at once, and the links between them, instead of trying to win only on a cheaper parts purchase.

sections.title: From diagram to habit, and the usual mistakes

blocks.text: After 1985 the value-chain diagram became classroom wallpaper. That popularity created a shallow version of the tool. Teams redraw the nine boxes, drop their department names into them, and stop. Porter's point was never the drawing. It was the search for activities that change price or cost, for linkages that amplify those activities, and for a configuration rivals cannot copy piecemeal.

Later strategy work kept returning to activities even when it used other labels. Core competence, covered in an earlier lesson, asks which capabilities underlie many products. Seven Powers asks which structural advantages protect profits. Playing to Win asks where to play and how to win. The value chain is the more microscopic map underneath those questions: if a competence or a power is real, it should show up as particular activities done differently, with particular links.

Two mistakes are common. The first is treating the chain as a cost-cutting checklist only. Differentiation also lives in activities: a luxury brand's service, packaging and store design are activities that support a higher price. The second is copying a celebrated step in isolation, such as flat packs without suburban car access, or a direct website without the inventory and supplier links that make direct selling cheap. Fit is the part that travels badly between firms.

Take a vintage resale project such as cool dairy. Write its value chain in plain language: how pieces are sourced and checked, photographed, stored, priced, listed, sold and shipped or handed over, and what happens with returns. Which activities create the buyer's willingness to pay, and which mainly add cost? Compared with a new-goods clothing shop, which steps should stay in-house, which could be handed to the customer or a partner, and which links (for example authentication before listing, or photography before storage) most need to fit together?

fun_fact.title: The table that would not fit in the car
fun_fact.text: Guinness World Records credits IKEA draughtsman Gillis Lundgren with inventing flatpack furniture in Älmhult in 1956, after he removed the legs of a table that would not fit in his car and took the idea to Ingvar Kamprad. IKEA Museum is more cautious: it says self-assembly tables such as DELFI, KÖKSA and RIGA were already in the 1953 catalogue, and that the leaf-shaped LÖVET table of 1955–56 was an early flat-packed piece but not the first. Either way, the cost idea is the same: stop shipping empty air, and let the customer finish the last step of operations at home.

glossary.explain: Porter's map of the primary and support activities a firm performs to design, make, sell, deliver and support its offer, used to find where advantage or waste sits.
The five direct activities in Porter's chain: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service.
The four activities that improve primary ones across the firm: firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development and procurement.
Activities that receive, store and handle inputs before operations begin.
Activities that transform inputs into the finished product or service.
Activities that store, pick and deliver the finished offer to buyers.
Activities that create demand and complete the sale, from pricing and advertising to channels and sales teams.
Post-sale activities that maintain or raise the product's value, such as support, repairs, returns and training.
General management systems such as planning, finance, quality and information management that support the whole chain.
Recruiting, hiring, training and other people practices that support every activity.
Know-how and process or product technology that improves activities across the firm, not only formal R&D.
Purchasing of inputs used across the firm, from raw materials to office equipment.
In Porter's diagram, the gap between the price buyers pay and the total cost of all value-chain activities.
Relationships between activities where the way one step is done changes the cost or effectiveness of another.
The larger chain that includes a firm's suppliers upstream and its distributors or retailers downstream.
Porter's 1985 Free Press book that introduced the value chain as a tool for finding sources of superior performance.
Porter's 1996 HBR article arguing that strategy is a unique configuration of interlocking activities, not just operational improvement.
Performing similar activities better than rivals; necessary, but easy to copy and not the same as strategy in Porter's 1996 sense.
The reinforcing match among a company's activity choices, so that copying only part of the system fails.
A map of a firm's important activities and how they connect to each other and to the value proposition.
A choice that rules out another incompatible choice; needed for a distinctive value chain.
Low-cost U.S. airline Porter uses to show a whole activity system: short hauls, one aircraft type, fast turns and limited frills.
Swedish furniture retailer whose low prices rest on linked choices such as flat packs, suburban warehouses and customer self-service.
Furniture shipped in compact cartons for customer assembly, cutting transport of empty space and shifting assembly cost to the buyer.
Founder of IKEA who scaled a furniture business around redesigned retail and logistics activities.
IKEA draughtsman credited by Guinness World Records with inventing flatpack furniture in 1956.
Inditex fashion brand that links store feedback, nearby production and frequent shipments to move designs to stores in weeks.
Spanish group that owns Zara and other chains; known for a fast, integrated apparel value chain.
Founder of Inditex.
Former Inditex CEO who said fashion stock goes bad quickly, so response time is the business.
PC company that in the 1990s sold direct and built to order, redesigning sales, inventory and supplier links together.
Founder of Dell Computer and voice of its late-1990s direct model in Magretta's HBR interview.
Magretta's term for coordinating suppliers, production and customers through information and schedules without owning every step.
Making a product after the customer order arrives, which can shrink finished-goods inventory when the chain is tightly linked.
Strategy writer and former HBR editor who explained Porter's tools for managers and interviewed Michael Dell.
Magretta's 2011 HBR Press book that walks through value chains, trade-offs and activity-system maps with IKEA and related cases.
Porter's 1980 industry framework; companion to the value chain, which looks inside the firm rather than only at industry pressure.
Prahalad and Hamel's idea of underlying capabilities; in value-chain terms, competences should show up as distinctive activities.
Huiru's vintage resale project, used here as a small-shop test case for mapping a value chain.
